Rebuilding the Foundations of Logic:
      Sets, Type Theory, and Reproducibility
               Developed from Pop, Refuse, Bind, and Collapse

                                   Flyxion
                                 Independent Researcher

                               October 2026


                                   Abstract
     Three foundational vocabularies dominate current practice:  first-order logic with its
     Boolean semantics, Zermelo–Fraenkel set theory with choice (ZFC), and the dependent
      type theories implemented in proof assistants such as Lean. They are usually intro-
     duced separately, with separate primitives and separate informal pictures of what a
      mathematical object is. This monograph rebuilds all three from one small base. The
      base is four operators, Pop (introduce a distinguished item), Refuse (restrict a domain
       of admissible items), Bind (relate or abstract over items), and Collapse (evaluate or
       identify). With these operators the untyped lambda calculus is recovered by renaming,
      the classical and intuitionistic propositional logics appear as two disciplines of Refuse,
      the axioms of ZFC appear as closure conditions on the four operators, and the kernel
       of a Lean-style dependent type theory appears as the internalization of Refuse inside
      Bind. The development includes the missing floors: first-order logic with structures, sat-
       isfaction and soundness; simply typed lambda calculus with an explicit Curry–Howard
      theorem; a worked derivation in the kernel; and the diagonal arguments of Cantor,
       Russell, and Gödel, kept distinct. Reproducibility is treated as part of the foundations:
      each statement carries a status label, each verified theorem is reported with its axiom
       footprint, and the layers at which a formal statement can fail are classified, so that
     a reader can tell what was established, relative to what, and by what kind of check.
     The axioms of ZFC, and the axioms added to a kernel, are treated as conventions:
      arbitrary at the base, and valuable because they give everyone a common language in
     which results can be checked, combined, and reused. Each chapter separates what is
      defined, what is proved here, what is cited from the literature, and what is only an
      analogy. The aim is a single ground-up account in which the differences between the
      three foundations are located precisely, at the point where each decides how Refuse
    may be used.

1  Scope, conventions, and status vocabulary

1.1 What this document is

The text develops a common base for logic, sets, and types, and then reads three standard
systems off that base. It is not a new foundation intended to compete with them. Its claim
is more modest: the three standard systems differ mainly in where they permit a domain
to be restricted, and a four-operator vocabulary makes that difference easy to state.

1.2  Status vocabulary

Every numbered statement carries one of the following labels, and the label is part of the
claim.

 Label              Meaning
  Definition       A stipulation. It can be adopted or declined but not refuted.
 Theorem,  Proposi-  Proved in this text, or proved by a short argument given in full.
  tion, Lemma, Corol-
  lary
 Cited result         Proved in the literature and used here without reproof. A refer-
                      ence is always given.
 Computation     A finite calculation whose script is reproduced in an appendix and
                    was run. It supports the stated instances only.
 Design rule      A choice made for convenience or to match a standard system.
 Analogy        A structural resemblance. It organizes understanding and proves
                       nothing.

                       proved.

1.3  Scope and warrant

Two things are kept apart throughout. The scope of a result is the set of objects it is
about: for example, a theorem about subsets of a fixed carrier is not a theorem about all
collections. The warrant of a result is the kind of support it has: a proof, a citation, or an
analogy. A theorem keeps the scope of its hypotheses; an analogy has no scope beyond the
sentence that states it. When a reading of one system in terms of another is offered, the
text says which of the two it is.

1.4  Content of a correspondence

Design rule 1.1 (Content of a correspondence). An operator correspondence has mathe-
matical content only when its domain, its interpretation, and the structure it preserves are
specified. Otherwise it is notation or analogy.

Every correspondence offered in this text is labeled accordingly: a Theorem or Proposition
when the three are given and a preservation result is proved, and an Analogy when they
are not. Section 18 gives the smallest complete example.

2  Pops, worlds, and the four operators

2.1 An informal picture

A mathematical activity begins by distinguishing something from its surroundings. That
act is Pop.  It continues by deciding which items count as admissible for the question at
hand, and by excluding the rest. That act is Refuse. Admissible items are then related to
each other, composed, paired, or abstracted over: Bind. Finally, related items are evaluated
or identified, so that different presentations of the same thing become one: Collapse. The
rest of the document makes these four sentences precise.

2.2  The domain layer

Definition 2.1 (Worlds and operators). Fix a set U. For a ∈U, P ⊆U, worlds Ω, Ω1, Ω2 ⊆
U, a relation R ⊆U × U, and an equivalence relation ∼on Ω, define

                   Pop(a) := {a},

                RefuseP (Ω) := Ω\ P,
             BindR(Ω1, Ω2) := R ∩(Ω1 × Ω2),     Bind(Ω1, Ω2) := Ω1 × Ω2,

pairs (a world over            U × U, which is again a carrier of items after a choice of pairing), and

Item (iv) is the first place where the rest of the document will branch.  In the Boolean
setting it says that refusing a refusal, relative to a fixed world, returns what one started
with. In Section 5 the same operator is shown to fail this law in a topological setting, and
the failure is exactly the failure of excluded middle.
Proposition 2.3 (Collapse is the universal identification). Let ∼be an equivalence relation
on a world Ωand q : Ω→Ω/∼the quotient map. For every function f  : Ω→X that is
constant on ∼-classes there is a unique ¯f : Ω/∼→X with ¯f ◦q = f.

Proof. Define ¯f([x]) := f(x). This is well defined because f is constant on classes. Unique-
ness holds because q is surjective.

Proposition 2.3 is the whole content of “Collapse as evaluation”: a computation that yields
the same result on equivalent presentations descends to the identified object. The same
universal property reappears in Section 11.7 as the rule for quotient types.

2.3 Why four

Analogy 2.4. The four operators correspond, in order, to introducing a variable or con-
stant, forming a subtype or subset, forming a function space or relation, and reducing a term
or forming a quotient. The correspondence is not claimed to be forced. Any presentation
of logic needs some way of introducing items, restricting their range, relating them, and
identifying them, and these are the four ways chosen here.

3  The term layer: Bind and Collapse give the lambda calcu-
    lus

3.1  Syntax and reduction

Definition 3.1 (SP terms). Let X be a countable set of variables. The set Tm of SP
terms is generated by

                            t, u ::= x  | Bind x. t  | Collapse(t, u),    x ∈X.

Variables are pops introduced by the context. The term Bind x. t binds the pop x in t,
and Collapse(t, u) asks that t be evaluated against u. Free variables, α-equivalence, and
capture-avoiding substitution t[x := u] are defined as for the lambda calculus. The single
reduction rule is
                           Collapse((Bind x. t), u) −→t[x := u]              (Collapse-β)
closed under all term contexts. Write ↠for its reflexive transitive closure.
Proposition 3.2 (The SP calculus is the lambda calculus). The map τ  : Tm →Λ into
the untyped lambda terms, τ(x) = x, τ(Bind x. t) = λx.τ(t), τ(Collapse(t, u)) = τ(t) τ(u),
is a bijection that preserves and reflects one-step reduction.  In particular, ↠on Tm is
confluent (Church–Rosser) and every theorem about β-reduction in Λ holds for Collapse-β.

Proof. τ is a bijection of grammars, clause by clause, and commutes with substitution by
induction on t. Hence t →u iff τ(t) →β τ(u). Confluence of →β is the Church–Rosser
theorem, proved for example in Barendregt [4, Ch. 3].

9.4  Relation to Refuse

Two of the instances bear on the central distinction of this text. The Russell argument fails
to produce a set only when the domain of the restriction is not itself a set (Design rule 8.4).
Cantor’s theorem shows that, over any domain A, the supply of Refuse outputs P(A)
strictly exceeds the supply of elements, which is why the Power set axiom is a substantive
axiom beyond Separation, and why a countable model cannot contain all of the refusals
available externally (Remark 9.6). In type theory the type-of-types paradox plays the role
of Russell’s: an unrestricted formation rule is inconsistent, and the universe hierarchy of
Section 11 is the restriction that blocks it.
Remark 9.6 (Skolem’s observation in operator terms). By Cited results 8.12(a) and 7.10,
if ZFC is consistent it has a countable model M. Inside M the Power set axiom holds, so
M contains an element which M regards as the set of all subsets of ω and, by Cantor’s
theorem (Theorem 9.3), as uncountable. From outside, D is countable, so this set has
countably many members. There is no contradiction: Power set asserts closure under the
Refuse-outputs that exist in M (Proposition 8.8), not under all of them. A first-order
theory cannot fix the full supply of refusals; this is the content of the contrast between
Separation and Power set drawn in Section 8.

Proof. Both statements are immediate from the recursive definition: the footprint of d is
the union of the axioms occurring in d with the footprints of the declarations d uses, and
a term whose footprint is empty is, after unfolding, a term built from the kernel rules
alone.

Footprints make precise a distinction that is often blurred. Whether a statement “needs
choice” is a property of a particular proof term, not of the statement. A function that
selects the first element of a nonempty list has an empty footprint, because the list supplies
the selection by data; a function that selects an element from a type known only to be
Nonempty has Classical.choice in its footprint, because nothing supplies the selection. Both
are “choose an element of a nonempty collection,” and only the second is the Axiom of
Choice in the sense of Proposition 8.9.
Design rule 12.4 (Report footprints). A formal development should state the footprint
of each headline theorem, in the manner of a list of axioms, so that a reader can see which
of the revisions of Section 14 the result depends on.

14  Revising the admissibility rule

14.1  The operator A

The four operators act within a fixed rule of admissibility. Foundations change when the
rule itself changes.

Definition 14.1 (Revision). A rule-set  is a theory T in a fixed language (axioms and
inference rules). A revision A is a map from rule-sets to rule-sets. The revisions considered
here add an axiom: Aσ(T) = T + σ.

Examples already encountered are σ = AC over ZF; σ = Classical.choice or σ = propext
over the kernel; and σ = “an inaccessible cardinal exists” over ZFC, with its type-theoretic
counterpart, one more universe level.
Proposition 14.2 (Revision and independence). If T is consistent and T ⊬σ and T ⊬¬σ,
then Aσ(T) and A¬σ(T) are both consistent and neither is contained in the other.

Proof. If T + σ were inconsistent then T ⊢¬σ, contrary to hypothesis; symmetrically for
T + ¬σ. If T + σ ⊇T + ¬σ in provable consequences then T + σ ⊢¬σ, so T + σ would be
inconsistent; and conversely.

By Cited result 8.10, AC over ZF satisfies the hypotheses of Proposition 14.2 whenever ZF
is consistent.
Combined with Cited result 8.12, this says that no sufficiently strong foundation can certify
from within the soundness of a revision that raises its own consistency strength. Statements
of the form “this system is justified” are therefore always made from a stronger vantage
point, or are not made at all. The honest form of a foundational claim is relative:  this
theorem is derivable in T, whose footprint is F, and T is consistent relative to T ′.

15  Where a statement can fail

A formal statement passes through several stages before it counts as established, and it can
fail at each. The classification below is generic and applies to any proof assistant with a
kernel.
Definition 15.1 (Failure layers).   (1) Parsing: the text is not a well-formed expression
      of the surface language.
  (2) Elaboration: the expression is parsed but cannot be completed to a well-typed term;
      implicit arguments, coercions, universe levels, or the expected sort of a position cannot
     be resolved.
  (3) Tactic or proof search: elaboration succeeds but a proof step does not close its goal.
  (4) Kernel: a fully elaborated term is rejected by the independent checker.
  (5) Derived contradiction: the term is accepted, and what it proves is inconsistent with
      the intended reading, for example because an assumption is inconsistent.
  (6) Scope: everything is accepted and consistent, but the theorem does not state what
       its informal description says it states.
Example 15.2 (Two elaboration failures). (i) A position that requires a proposition is
given a value: ∀n : N, n ≤2 →0. The final 0 has type N, but the arrow expects a type
or a proposition there. This fails at layer (2). (ii) A proposition is passed to a function on
booleans: with not : Bool →Bool and ¬ : Prop →Prop distinct, the expression not (n ≤2)
expects a Bool and receives a Prop. This also fails at layer (2). The usual repair is to use
¬, or to insert a decision procedure that converts the proposition to a boolean.

                                       28

Analogy 15.3 (Proof checking as a fifth operator). Layers (2) through (4) together play the
role of a Verify step that follows Bind and precedes Collapse in the lifecycle used elsewhere
in the Spherepop program: a term is built, its admissibility is checked, and only then is it
evaluated or identified. This is a resemblance of order only.

The layers are ordered by how much of the argument has been tested: a layer-(1) or (2)
failure says nothing about the mathematics, because the statement was never in a form
the system could examine; a layer-(5) failure says the theorem is vacuous or false as stated;
a layer-(6) failure says the formalization is correct and its meaning is not.  Reports of
“verified” results should name the layer at which the check was passed.
Proposition 15.4 (A verified theorem is relative to its axioms). If d is accepted by the
kernel with footprint F = Ax(d), then d is a theorem of the kernel extended by F.  In
particular, a statement obtained as a theorem about hypotheses supplied as declared axioms
is a theorem of the form “if the axioms then the conclusion,” and its footprint contains
those axioms.

Proof. By Proposition 12.3, every axiom used by d lies in F, so d is derivable in the kernel
with F added. For the second sentence, an axiom α declared by the author and used in
the proof of d occurs in Ax(d) by definition.

Proposition 15.4 is elementary and is the formal content of the slogan that a derivation
cannot be more informative than its premises.  It is worth stating because it separates
two readings of a verified result: the conclusion holds and the conclusion follows from the
declared axioms. Only the second is established.

16  Conventions as a common language

16.1  The role of an arbitrary base

The axioms of ZFC are not forced.  Independence results (Cited result 8.10) show that
Choice can be added or its negation added, with both extensions consistent if ZF is. The
same is true of the Continuum Hypothesis over ZFC [6]. In that precise sense the choice of
base is a convention, comparable to the choice of a unit of length: a different unit would
do equally well as far as nature is concerned, and no measurement is more correct for being
in metres.
What a convention provides is not truth but comparability. Two parties who have adopted
the same base can exchange statements and derivations, and each can check what the other
produced. The value of ZFC, and of a fixed kernel with a fixed set of added axioms, is that
it supplies one rule of admissibility, stated in advance, that everyone can apply. The rest
of this section makes the point exact.

16.2  Reproducible results

Definition 16.1 (Reproducible result). Let T be a theory with a decidable set of axioms.
A reproducible result relative to T  is a triple (T, ϕ, d) where d is a finite derivation of the
sentence ϕ from the axioms of T.
Cited result 16.2 (Checkability). For a first-order theory with a decidable set of axioms,
the relation “d is a derivation of ϕ from T” is decidable. See Enderton [10, Ch. 2 and 3].

                                       29

Cited result 16.2 is the logical content of the word reproducible in this text:  given the
base, the question whether a purported derivation is correct has a mechanical answer that
does not depend on who asks. The kernel of a proof assistant is an implementation of this
decision procedure for a particular base. (For the full Lean kernel the situation is subtler,
as noted in Cited result 11.8, and this text claims only what the cited sources claim.)
Proposition 16.3 (Results compose over a common base). (a) If (T, ϕ, d) and (T, ϕ →ψ, e)
are reproducible results then so is (T, ψ, d ∗e), where d ∗e concatenates the derivations
and applies modus ponens.  (b) If T ⊆T ′ and (T, ϕ, d) is reproducible, then (T ′, ϕ, d) is
reproducible.

Proof. (a) The concatenation is a finite sequence each of whose lines is an axiom of T or
follows from earlier lines, ending in ψ. (b) Every axiom of T  is an axiom of T ′, so d is a
derivation from T ′.

Proposition 16.3(a) is what a common base buys:  derivations from the same T can be
chained without translation.  Part (b) says that results are portable upward:  a result
proved over a weaker base remains valid over any stronger one. The converse fails, which
is why a footprint matters (Definition 12.2).
Example 16.4 (Results that cannot be combined). Let T1 = ZF+AC and T2 = ZF+¬AC.
If ZF is consistent, each of T1 and T2 is consistent (Cited result 8.10), so each supports
many reproducible results. But T1 ∪T2 proves both AC and ¬AC and so proves every
sentence. A reproducible result relative to T1 and one relative to T2 cannot be chained in
either theory in the manner of Proposition 16.3(a), and the pair says nothing jointly. A
community in which half the authors assumed T1 and half T2, without saying so, would
produce correct and mutually unusable results.
Example 16.4 is the formal reason that an arbitrary base is better than a different base for
each author. The choice among conventions is not forced, but the existence of one agreed
convention is what lets results be collected, compared, and reused.
Analogy 16.5 (Units, formats, and protocols). A unit of length, a character encoding,
and a network protocol share one feature: any particular choice could have been otherwise,
and what matters is that a single choice is widely adopted and written down. Foundations
of mathematics are a convention of this kind with an unusually long track record. The
analogy proves nothing about mathematics; it says what role the convention plays.

17  Arbitrary bases, determinate consequences

17.1  Arbitrary at the base, forced above it

That the base is a convention does not make its consequences conventional. Once a base T
is fixed, whether T ⊢ϕ is a matter of fact, settled by a derivation or by an independence
proof. Two layers must be kept apart:
  • the choice of T is not forced and is not true or false;
  • what follows from T is determinate, and statements about it are true or false.
A claim of the form “the Axiom of Choice is arbitrary” is correct about the first layer and
says nothing about the second. A claim of the form “therefore anything derived from it is
arbitrary” confuses the two.

                                       30

17.2 How much does the convention matter?

The choice matters little for some statements and a great deal for others, and both facts
are theorems.
Cited result 17.1 (Conservativity for arithmetic). ZF and ZFC prove the same Π12 sentences;
in particular they prove the same arithmetical sentences. This follows from Gödel’s con-
structible universe together with Shoenfield absoluteness. See Jech [13, Ch. 13 and Ch. 25].
So adopting Choice never changes which arithmetical statements are provable. It changes
what can be proved about large infinite objects.


                                               RCited result 17.2 (Choice and measurability). In ZFC there is a subset of   that is not
Lebesgue measurable (Vitali). Relative to the consistency of an inaccessible cardinal, ZF
with dependent choice is consistent with every set of reals being Lebesgue measurable
(Solovay [17]).
Cited result 17.2 shows that the choice of convention can have visible consequences in
analysis.  It also shows that the consequence is itself determinate:  given the base, the

17.3 What a convention can be assessed on

Design rule 17.3 (Assessing a convention). A foundational base is assessed on four things,
none of which is truth:
   (i) Consistency relative to other bases (Section 13);
  (ii) Strength: whether the mathematics to be done can be carried out in it;
  (iii) Conservativity: which statements it leaves unchanged relative to a weaker base, as in
     Cited result 17.1;
 (iv) Adoption: how many parties use it, since that is what gives comparability.
Remark 17.4. This does not make the choice of base unconstrained. A base that is incon-
sistent has no use as a common language, since it proves every sentence. A base too weak
to express the statements parties wish to exchange is not a common language for them.
Adoption alone decides between bases that satisfy the other three equally well.

18.1  Representation systems and canonical forms

The earlier sections distinguish a convention from what follows from it. A numeral system
is the simplest place to see the distinction proved rather than asserted, because the object
represented (a natural number) is fixed in advance and the representation is a free choice.
Definition 18.1 (Representation system). A representation system is a triple (R, [[·]], →)
of a set R of inscriptions, a denotation map [[·]] : R →X into a set X of represented objects,
and a rewriting relation →on R.  It is sound  if r →r′ implies  [[r]] = [[r′]], terminating if
there is no infinite chain r0 →r1 →· · · , and confluent if r ↠s and r ↠t imply a common
u with s ↠u and t ↠u. A normal form is an inscription with no outgoing rewrite.

Theorem 18.2 (Canonical forms). Let (R, [[·]], →) be sound and terminating.
  (a) Every r ∈R rewrites to some normal form nf(r) with [[nf(r)]] = [[r]].

     normal form, and for all r, r′ ∈R,

                                                         [[r]] = [[r′]] ⇐⇒nf(r) = nf(r′).

Proof. (a) By termination, any maximal chain from r is finite and ends in a normal form;
by soundness the denotation is constant along the chain. (b) Two normal forms reachable

termination, soundness, and injectivity on normal forms are available. The three properties
together say that the representation is a presentation of the object and not a different object,
and that a canonical representative can be reached by any strategy.

  (5) the scope: a plain-language statement of what the theorem asserts, including what it
     does not;
  (6) the environment: pinned versions of the tools and libraries, so that the check can be
      repeated.

Items (1) to (3) are what turn “verified” into a claim that can be checked. Item (4) is
the one most often omitted. A development in which the substantive assumptions enter as
declared axioms is still a correct derivation, and by Proposition 15.4 what it establishes is
the implication from those axioms. Reporting them separately lets a reader judge whether
the axioms are the content of the claim.

19.2  Controls

Definition 19.2 (Controls). A negative control is a statement that is known to be false or
ill-formed and that the pipeline must reject. A positive control is a statement known to be
provable that the pipeline must accept.
Proposition 19.3 (A negative control detects trivial acceptance). Suppose a checking
pipeline accepts every derivation of ⊥from its base. Then it accepts every sentence ϕ with
a one-line extension of that derivation. Hence a pipeline that rejects a single known-false
sentence has not accepted a derivation of ⊥.

Proof. From a derivation d of ⊥, adding the step ⊥→ϕ (ex falso) and modus ponens gives
a derivation of ϕ for any ϕ. Contrapositively, if some known-false sentence is rejected, then
no derivation of ⊥was accepted, assuming the pipeline accepts all correct derivations from
its base.

Controls test the pipeline, not the theorem. They are cheap and they exclude a class of
silent failures, in particular a pipeline that accepts everything.

19.3 What reproducibility does not give

   (i) It does not give truth about the subject matter. A result relative to T is a fact about
      derivability from T.
  (ii) It does not give consistency. By Gödel’s second theorem (Cited result 9.1), a base
      strong enough for arithmetic cannot certify its own consistency; consistency is relative,
      as in Cited result 13.1.
 (iii) It does not give interpretation. A formalization can be accepted by the kernel and
        still fail to state what its authors say it states (layer (6) of Definition 15.1).
Analogy 19.4 (Common language). The three limits are the limits of any shared standard.
A common unit does not tell one what to measure; a common character encoding does not
tell one what to write; a common base does not tell one what is true. What each does
is make it possible for a second party to repeat the first party’s step and see the same
outcome.

20 A reading of the RSVP plenum

20.1  Purpose and status

The author’s RSVP framework describes a plenum Ψ = (Φ, v, S) consisting of a scalar field
Φ, a vector (transport) field v, and an entropy field S, from which gravity-like effects are
proposed to emerge as an entropic descent, with a compact form G = −∇S + ξ∇Φ. This
section asks only whether the four operators supply a useful vocabulary for the plenum.
Nothing in this section derives the field equations of the plenum from the operators. What
is proved is one general fact about identification and information (Proposition 20.2); the
remaining statements are labeled Analogy or Conjecture and carry no more warrant than
that.

20.3 What is lost by identification

Collapse identifies items.  Identification forgets which of the identified items was present.
A quantitative form of this statement holds in any finite setting and is the only theorem
needed.

Proposition 20.2 (Information lost by Collapse). Let Ωbe a finite world with a probability
measure µ, let X be the random item with law µ, let ∼be an equivalence relation on Ωand
q : Ω→Ω/∼the quotient map, and write H for Shannon entropy. Define the lost entropy
L(∼) := H(X) −H(q(X)). Then

                         L(∼) = H X | q(X) ≥0,

with equality if and only if every ∼-class contains at most one item of positive probability.
Moreover, if ∼1 refines ∼2 then L(∼1) ≤L(∼2), and

                      L(∼2) = L(∼1) + H q1(X) | q2(X)  .

Proof. Since q(X)  is a function of X, H(X, q(X)) = H(X).  The chain rule gives
H(X, q(X)) =  H(q(X)) + H(X   |  q(X)),  hence L(∼) = H(X   |  q(X)),  which
is  nonnegative  as a  conditional  entropy.    It  vanishes   iff,  given  the  class, X  is
determined  almost  surely,  that  is   iff  each  class  has  at most one  point  of  posi-
tive  probability.   For the refinement statement,  q2 =  r ◦q1  for a function  r,  so
H(X  | q2(X)) = H(X, q1(X)  | q2(X)) = H(q1(X)  | q2(X)) + H(X  | q1(X), q2(X)),
and H(X   | q1(X), q2(X)) = H(X   | q1(X)) because q2(X)  is determined by q1(X).
Nonnegativity of H(q1(X) | q2(X)) gives monotonicity.

Proposition 20.2 is an instance of the data-processing principle.  Its role here is to give
a precise, nonnegative, additive quantity attached to a Collapse: how much of the item’s
identity is not recoverable from its class. Coarser Collapse loses at least as much, and the
loss composes additively along a chain of refinements.

20.4 An analogy and a conjecture

Analogy 20.3 (Entropy as the cost of Collapse). In the plenum, the entropy field S
and the “entropic descent” of the framework have the same shape as Proposition 20.2: a
coarse description discards information, the discarded amount is a nonnegative quantity
that grows with coarseness, and systems under a coarsening flow move in the direction
in which it grows. This resemblance suggests reading S as the lost entropy of a Collapse
determined by the scale at which the plenum is described.
Conjecture 20.4 (Plenum entropy as lost entropy). There is a family of equivalence
relations {∼λ}λ on the configuration space of the plenum, indexed by a scale λ and refining
as λ decreases, such that the pointwise lost entropy Sλ(x) := L(∼λ) restricted to the cell at
x agrees, in the continuum limit and up to normalization, with the entropy field S of the
framework, and such that −∇Sλ reproduces the entropic drift term of G.

Evidence. Only the structural resemblance of Analogy 20.3. The conjecture is heuristic.
It is also easy to falsify in principle, because it requires an explicit choice of {∼λ} and a
comparison with the field equations of the framework.

20.5  Implications if the conjecture held

The implications listed are conditional, and each depends on Conjecture 20.4.
   (i) No extra primitive. The entropic term would be a property of the Collapse family
     and would not require a separate entropy primitive in the ontology.

(ii) Additivity across scales.  Proposition 20.2 gives S an additive decomposition along

from fractions import Fraction as F
import itertools, math, random

def uni(n):                      # exploding-dot normal form, digits low to high
    b = [n]; i = 0
    while i < len(b):
        while b[i] >= 3:
            q = b[i] // 3
            b[i] -= 3 * q
            if i + 1 == len(b): b.append(0)
            b[i + 1] += 2 * q
        i += 1
    while len(b) > 1 and b[-1] == 0: b.pop()
    return ''.join(map(str, reversed(b)))

def val(s):
    return sum(int(c) * F(3, 2) ** k for k, c in enumerate(reversed(s)))

assert all(val(uni(n)) == n for n in range(3000))            # value conserved
for l in range(1, 10):                                        # injectivity
    seen = {}
    for t in itertools.product('012', repeat=l):
        if t[0] == '0' and l > 1: continue
        v = val(''.join(t)); assert v not in seen; seen[v] = t
